{"docket_number": "24-1063", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "2025", "first_party": "Munson P. Hunter", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "United States of America", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit", "argued": ["2026-03-03T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

1. Does an appeal waiver bar all claims except for ineffective assistance of counsel or a sentence exceeding the statutory maximum? 

2. Does such a waiver become ineffective if the sentencing judge later tells the defendant they can appeal, and the government fails to object?

 

", "facts_of_the_case": "

Munson P. Hunter, III pleaded guilty to committing wire fraud affecting a financial institution and to aiding and abetting. A federal district court sentenced him to 51 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release. A specific condition of that supervised release requires Hunter to take any mental health medication prescribed by his physician.

Hunter challenged his sentence at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, arguing the medication condition infringed on his due process liberty interests and that the written judgment improperly included the “aiding and abetting” reference. The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal regarding the medication condition, finding it was barred by an appeal waiver in Hunter's plea agreement, and affirmed the judgment, noting that the “aiding and abetting” charge was indeed part of the count to which Hunter pleaded guilty.

", "conclusion": "

When a criminal defendant signs an appeal waiver as part of a plea agreement — a promise not to challenge a future sentence — that waiver becomes unenforceable if enforcing it would produce a miscarriage of justice, meaning it would lock in place an egregious sentencing error so obvious and extreme that it would bring the judicial system into disrepute. Justice Elena Kagan authored the 8-1 majority opinion.

A district court must affirmatively accept a plea agreement before it takes effect, and an appeals court holds exclusive control over whether to enforce the waiver — meaning a court's decision to enforce a waiver directly cements a sentence in place, lawful or not. Because courts sit at the center of approving and implementing these agreements from start to finish, they carry an institutional responsibility for the results. Federal courts have a recognized independent interest in ensuring that legal proceedings appear fair; automatically enforcing appeal waivers without exception would risk allowing obviously lawless sentences to stand, which would damage public confidence in the judiciary. That institutional responsibility means the parties' agreement alone cannot be the final word.

The miscarriage-of-justice standard sets a deliberately high bar: ordinary sentencing errors — mistakes in calculating a guidelines range or weighing sentencing factors — cannot overcome a valid waiver, because routine errors do not discredit the courts and because a looser standard would undermine the value of appeal waivers in plea negotiations. Only obvious, egregious errors qualify. Non-exhaustive examples include a sentence that exceeds what the relevant statute permits, a sentence infected with a blatant constitutional violation such as a judge using race as a factor or imposing a constitutionally invalid supervised release condition, and a sentence imposed without any minimum of civilized procedure. Because the Fifth Circuit never applied this standard to Hunter's challenge to the mandatory-medication condition, the case returns to that court to resolve whether his appeal waiver should be set aside.

- Justice Neil Gorsuch concurred (joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Jackson), arguing that today's ruling is an important but incomplete correction to the Court's long history of enabling coercive plea bargaining, and suggesting that lower courts should apply the miscarriage-of-justice exception broadly to include plain guidelines errors, substantively unreasonable sentences, and conditions of supervised release wholly unrelated to legitimate sentencing purposes, while also questioning whether appeal waivers may be fundamentally problematic as prospective waivers of statutory rights.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh concurred (joined by Justices Samuel Alito and Amy Coney Barrett), writing separately to emphasize that the majority establishes a genuinely high bar limited to extreme and egregious cases, and to flag his disagreement with Justice Gorsuch's concurrence as potentially setting a lower threshold than the majority intends.

Justice Barrett concurred, writing to clarify that the decision rests on longstanding procedural common law principles governing waiver rather than on the Court's supervisory power over inferior federal courts, a power she views skeptically.

Justice Clarence Thomas dissented, arguing that Hunter's knowing and voluntary appeal waiver is a valid, bargained-for relinquishment of a statutory right and must be enforced, that the majority identifies no constitutional text, statute, or established common-law doctrine to support its new miscarriage-of-justice exception, and that the decision amounts to unlawful policymaking that will flood courts with meritless appeals and erode the value of plea agreements for defendants.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We will hear argument this morning in Case 24-1063, Hunter versus United States. Ms. Blatt. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: All contracts are subject to defenses. So appeal waivers are also subject to defenses and can be excused in more circumstances than the two recognized below. The government argues that no contract defense can apply to knowing and voluntary appeal waivers, no exceptions. But, if appeal waivers bind defendants under contract principles, they can be excused under contract principles. A contrary approach is anathema to our criminal justice system. No appeal for sentences above the statutory maximum based on race, religion, national origin, tribal status, or pure vindictiveness. No appeal for pregnancy bans, castration, or compelled church attendance either. These scenarios are all real cases. Or take this case. Only the most paramount government interest overcomes the fundamental right to refuse medical treatment. But Hunter was sentenced to a mandatory medical condition even though he had no mental health issues, let alone one connected to the crime or related to any sentencing goal. Defendants bargain for caps on their sentencing exposure. Those bargains are destroyed by plainly unlawful sentences that are totally outside the realm of plausibility of either party. Now floodgates concerns are belied by decades of experience in the 11 circuits that reject the Fifth Circuit's rule. Applying defenses to appeal waivers maintains the status quo. Contract defenses are narrow by design and rarely satisfied. Appeal waivers will continue to bar the vast majority of alleged sentencing errors, guidelines miscalculations, insufficient explanation, or misbalancing under 3553(a). But contract defenses may be satisfied in the rare case of clear legal error and punishment unauthorized by statute or that violates the Constitution. At a minimum, this Court should remand on the second question presented. I welcome questions. Ms. Blatt, if you can waive constitutional rights or statutory rights, why can't you waive these contractually rights that are statutory here? You absolutely can waive the -- the -- the right to appeal and there's a appeal agreement, but the issue here is, absent this plea agreement, which is a contract, the defendant could just walk away. The only thing that is binding him to the waiver, and the government is asserting, the enforceability of the appeal waiver by contract. I don't think there's any dispute that the plea agreement is a contract. If you waive your right to trial when you -- at -- at the arraignment and just say I waive my fundamental right to trial, that's a pretty big waiver. Tomorrow, you can get up and say, you know what, Judge, I think I want a jury trial. You can just revoke it. But, here, there's a plea agreement. There's a contract. The government has to rely on the contract principles. The government gets out of plea agreements by relying on contract defenses. And there's just no rational -- or it's just inexplicable that you would not apply contract defenses to this contract when you do to all others. Could -- in this case, could the government simply void the agreement and proceed with the 10 counts? Yeah, I -- I don't think so, but here's why. The government has in many cases asserted frustration of purpose and did exactly what you said. I think, here, because the government has no interest and is not defending the mandatory medication condition, there's just no countervailing principles. Now the government has not disputed it can allege a breach of the plea agreement, and that would result in an invalidation of the plea. The government just doesn't dispute that. That's why defendants so rarely bring these appeals, is because they run a substantial risk of exactly what you're saying. We would try to argue that there's no breach based on the fact that the judge told him he had a right to appeal. And even if it is a breach, you know, it's -- it's justified by defending the contract exception, and the government doesn't have any countervailing interest to invalidate the whole agreement. And that's all the stuff we would fight on remand. Here, we're cut off because the -- the Fifth Circuit has this categorical rule that, although it's a contract and you're denied the benefit of the bargain with sentences that exceed the statutory maximum, it allows no other exceptions. Counsel, it seems to me that you're really asking for an equivalent of a Miranda warning that somebody would have to give, the -- the prosecutor, maybe even the judge, going through all the things that you're required to. What -- what exactly -- what are the elements of what they must -- you must tell the -- the defendant so long as you -- so that you don't leave any, you know, strings untied? So there's a distinction between the first question presented and the second question presented. If the judge said absolutely nothing, we'd still be here on a contract defense. There's no warnings. It's just there's 30 years of -- actually, 34 years where this has been the law. We think, in terms of the second question presented, all the judge has to say is that you had -- you may have a right to appeal; you should look at your plea agreement. That's it. There's no other warnings. There's no nothing. So that's the second question presented, but on the first question presented, we're just arguing there's -- the government is enforcing the plea waiver. We're saying it's subject to one of contract defenses or a miscarriage-of-justice exception. So that's all to brief on remand. This has nothing to do with what a court would have to -- to -- Well -- -- educate the defendant about. Well, I think it does have to do with that, and it seems to me that the court is the only one can do -- that can do it. You know, if you're the defense attorney, I don't know, you want to advise your client, of course, but, you know, if the judge says something that's not right, it seems to me that it's -- the lawyer's in a tough position because the judge has given them an opportunity to raise this after the fact if you think -- and so it would be odd, I think, for the lawyer to stand up and say, oh, Your Honor, remember you've got to tell him that he can't do this or this or, otherwise, it might not be valid. So, on the second question presented, we're literally arguing a straight litigation forfeiture waiver. All we're saying -- this is on the second question presented -- all courts hold what you just said except for the Ninth Circuit. It doesn't matter what the judge says, except the Ninth Circuit. What we're trying to argue on the second question presented is, when the judge said you have a right to appeal, given the back and forth on the medication condition, and when the prosecutor said, Your Honor, I believe, um -- well, I -- no, that he -- two things happened. One, the defendant detrimentally relied on that in bringing the appeal and exposed himself to a breach, and, two, and I think the better argument, is, had the prosecutor spoken up, we would not be wondering had the court imposed this bizarre medication condition thinking that there could be a right to appeal, and that's a simple remand. Well, that's kind of -- But the more important question is the first question presented, where all 11 circuits -- this has nothing to do with what -- what a court would advise. You just sign a plea agreement, and there are broad waivers and that's it. Defendants don't bring these because it's an alleged breach. You do have these rare exceptions where it can mean a contract defense or be a miscarriage of justice, the castration example, a pregnancy ban, the government's view, race, mandatory medication that tough, that -- that's it, you signed the appeal waiver. That's absurd when everyone from Elon Musk to billionaires to corporations to mom-and-pop -- mom-and-pops can assert contract defenses. The government doesn't even tell you why this contract, unlike any other contract in the entire universe, can't have a defense. Ms. -- Ms. Blatt, I guess I'm trying to figure out what the nature of your argument is. You refer to contract defenses. Then you say or a miscarriage-of- justice exception. In the time you've been up there, you've said the question is whether it's outside the realm of plausibility. You've referred to constitutional violations. Mm-hmm. I mean, when is it that this would come into play in your view more specifically? So, hopefully, almost never because courts don't do crazy things like here, but let me -- Well, but I'm asking for a standard. Sure. Like, what are we looking to? The -- the -- the standard is that the easiest and the high-level rule statement is it's subject to contract defenses. Well, I don't -- what -- So now I'm going to -- -- what is a contract defense? Does that just mean it's against public policy or -- No, I'm going to break that -- -- are you referring to other kinds of -- -- break that down. There are hundreds of years of precedent on very narrow defenses that sound maybe in label broad, but once you take off that label, they all have a thumb on the scale, exceedingly a thumb on the scale in favor of enforcement. That's why contract defenses are so rare. And if you go past the Restatements, you start reading why they're never applied, including public policy. Public policy, as this Court said in Rumery, the first public policy is enforcement of the contract. So you would have to have some really out there public policy that would outweigh that now. Is there -- is there anything other that you're -- than public policy that you're talking about -- No. I think -- -- when you refer to contract defenses? -- I think the one that makes -- public policy's a good one because it's rooted in this Court's case law. The one that makes the most sense is the one the government asserts, which is frustration of purpose. The government has gotten out of plea agreements in the two cases both in the Fifth Circuit and the Tenth Circuit because they said it was frustrated when a defendant didn't do anything wrong but just got out on collateral relief. Just -- so if I -- frustration of purpose, why I think it's the best and that's why I got the standard of outside the realm of plausibility. Ms. Blatt -- Well, Ms. Blatt, I -- I think you've got a strong argument on something like miscarriage of justice or something that's shockingly improper, something that would capture the examples that you started out with, where the -- the sentence is based on race or religion or something like that. I think you've got a -- a strong argument on that. When you go further, then I get nervous because public policy is very broad. Plea agreements have some attributes of a contract, but they're not just -- they're not like ordinary contracts. And the -- imposing the entire law of contracts here seems to me rather open-ended. So -- Okay. Then can you please say the entire law of contracts does not apply to the government? Because that's all they do is cite contract law in enforcing these plea agreements. So make sure you write your decision that they're not enforceable either under contract principles, that the government can't rely on it. It is a double standard, including in the Fifth Circuit. All right. Well, what do you in concrete terms, what do you think would -- the law of contracts would say about a variety of issues that might be waived? How about constitutional venue? I -- I don't know what you mean by that. Sixth Amendment venue. So all I'm talking -- The right to be tried in the -- So -- -- the state or district where the offense occurred. -- I mean, waiver, Mezzanatto, you have a million cases on waiver. In terms of -- this case involves no waiver of a trial right. This is involving a waiver of the right to appeal sentencing errors. And all -- the courts have generally said miscarriage of justice, but all of -- at least eight of them have said contract principles. What about the Sixth Amendment right to a speedy trial? Well, you have -- you have cases on all of this about the waiver has to be knowing and voluntary and then you have to decide if it's a personal right versus a public right. What about the suppression of evidence under the Fourth Amendment or the Sixth Amendment? You waive all that when you waive your right to trial. A defendant can almost never get out of a plea agreement. You've held back in, I think, '72 under Brady that plea agreements are binding and they waive the right. The only way to get out of a plea agreement -- So I -- I thought -- I thought the only thing -- -- you have cases on that, Lafler. You actually have Supreme Court cases that say you can almost never get out of a plea agreement. Ms. Blatt, I thought the only thing before us was waiver of sentencing errors. Correct. Not anything else. Correct. Because you have a million cases saying defendants can't get out of plea agreements. Yeah. And on -- on -- on -- on Justice Alito's point about whether these are ordinary contracts or not, if they're not, we might think about unconstitutional conditions doctrine in this area too. And I was a little surprised we didn't have more of that in the briefing before us, and I'm kind of curious why. I mean, as I understand it, the defendant here pleaded guilty to one count of fraud for $32,000. That was the only amount charged in the indictment. And then he wound up being sentenced for something like a half a million dollars worth of fraud and a whole bunch of other unindicted incidents. And it's not clear to me what benefit he got from his plea waiver -- appeal waiver, I should say, that would be proportionate and have a nexus to that additional right foregone. So let me just -- and I think this captures, Justice Alito, a lot of defendants are unhappy with their sentences, but when they're -- and they're mostly guidelines, but within -- when they're within the statutory maximum, courts have universally said tough luck, that part of the appeal waiver is the assumption that the court will make ordinary errors in sentencing guidelines as long as you're sentenced within the statutory maximum. The government's view is you can sentence someone for 30 years for a misdemeanor and there's no right to defense. Now they want to try to rely on maybe something in the contract, but that contract provision doesn't say what the government says. So -- nor the Fifth Circuit. The Fifth Circuit, I mean -- With respect, Ms. Blatt, do I get an answer to my question about why we don't have an unconstitutional condition? It -- the -- the sentence seemed to me, 51 months and all the fines, I -- I don't think he -- because we're just -- I mean, yeah, the defendant's not happy with his sentence. Most defendants aren't. But they're within the statutory maximum. So I think that's the answer. The condition of probation -- sorry, the condition of supervised release is the preposterous one that says you have to follow the recommendations. All right. In your -- One -- one might argue, though, that that's an unconstitutional condition to be required to give up a bodily -- a right of bodily integrity without a compelling showing by the government. Or any showing. Any showing. I mean, it's just totally bizarre. The government doesn't defend it. It's -- I'm going to get this example out. If there was a law that was passed that said all judges must take antidepressants recommended by their physician, I think you would find it stupidly unconstitutional and offensive. Well, I think we already have. I mean, we've got a very -- And it might be medically -- and it might be medically appropriate to take antidepressants. -- 50-year-old case -- It doesn't matter. But, Ms. -- Ms. Blatt, is the problem that you couldn't really raise Justice Gorsuch's very significant point because there is this waiver? Like, the unconstitutional condition, I think, is an argument that could be made in the context of an appeal when you were trying to say that the -- that the trial judge or the sentencing judge did something wrong. Yes. And -- But the problem is you have a waiver, so you never even get to raise that issue. Can't raise it. That's what I was trying to say to Justice Kagan. In the universe of reading all of these cases, the court of -- so, first of all, defendants don't bring them because they don't want to get turned around and have the plea agreement breached. The lawyers don't want to bring them because they've been sanctioned. And, third, the court of appeals don't want to see these cases because they have to deal with it. And that's why, when you read them, they say, this is going to be rarely applied, please don't bring them, it has to be an extreme case. Right. So is your issue -- Well, it might be rare, but, usually, you know, we have a standard, you know, what are those rare cases? How do we identify them? And that's what I'm trying to figure out. So -- Now you said, well, you could definitely argue if it's above the statutory maximum. But the Fifth Circuit actually seems to agree with you. So -- so, on that one, you're in the same place as the Fifth Circuit. So what else? And how do we identify these errors? And is it -- I guess maybe the backup point is, is this really a place where we should look to contract law, or is it a place where we should just say, yes, we should have an exception for, you know, miscarriages of justice and -- and people know what that means -- So -- -- and know that -- Yeah. And -- -- it refers only to extreme cases? And what I've distilled, which I think is a really good standard, is, first, the error has to be obvious, like clear and indisputable, like no even argument on the other side. It just has to be a really bad mistake, whether that's in excess of the statutory maximum, the case involving Judge Stras in the Eighth Circuit, it was a person who possessed a gun. The court imposed a very bizarre, unrelated, weird condition that he had a lifetime ban. It just kind of came out of nowhere. Those are clear errors. Now, once you get past clear error, like, if you're having an argument about it, the defendant is just going to lose. But, when it's a stupid clear error, that's one. That's the first gateway. The second gateway is exactly what you said. It's got to be really bad. And what I said what really bad means is it's just so plainly unauthorized by statute or a violation of a constitutional right, which covers race, First Amendment, religion, bodily integrity. Why -- But there is another option, isn't there, I mean, in addition to those possibilities for saying this waiver is unenforceable? Isn't there the option of saying that we really just don't allow these kinds of waivers? In other words, that, you know, it's not, for example, knowing and voluntary for a defendant to prospectively waive his right to object or to appeal a sentencing error. Yeah. And so they're just not enforceable. I know you don't make this argument -- No, but here's -- -- but there are -- there are -- No, I like it that you have a case kind of against me on it. So the -- the knowing and voluntary just says you have to know, you know, you know all about what the waiver of the right to mean. You don't have to know the consequences. So that's why. Now there are some -- Well, I understand, but there are -- there are district court judges, very thoughtful district court judges, who have accepted the view that this is different than a trial waiver that, you know, goes with your guilty plea -- Mm-hmm. -- that there's something unique about the prospective waiver of a sentencing proceeding that you know is going to happen, but you're giving up your right to appeal any errors with respect to that proceeding, that -- that that's just -- you can't knowingly -- So -- -- have that kind of waiver some courts have said. -- you're correct -- the Fourth Circuit in 2025 in a -- in a case, Smith, cited by Cato, does exactly what you said. It said this cannot possibly be a knowing and voluntary waiver, but we're going to also apply miscarriage of justice. So they did the two steps, but they said what you said. I just don't know if the rest of you would agree with that analysis, but they said -- Ms. -- Ms. Blatt -- What -- what are the -- -- exactly what you said. -- what are the specific exceptions that you would identify? Ineffective assistance of counsel? So that, yeah, goes to knowing and voluntary. Right. And then -- And a sentence exceeds the statutory maximum, right? Yes. And unconstitutional factors used in the sentence? Yeah. I would just call that violates the Constitution. Now -- Well, those are three. No, just two. Well, I listed three there, but -- Hold on. Let me just -- can I combine them into two? So the unauthorized by statute, the problem with the Fifth Circuit is, you know, you could have what that means. You could have restitution unauthorized by statute. In the case of the Eighth Circuit, they applied a lifetime ban on certain things for this gun. It was -- just unauthorized by the statute to me covers a little more than sentence -- sentences exceeding the maximum. Also, this condition of supervised release, if it was you have to go to church, it's just -- it's not allowed by statute. It's just -- and it's plainly unconstitutional. Well, supervised release conditions, I think, do present a different bucket, and I just wonder -- They do. -- how would you characterize what the exception -- Oh. Are just -- -- for conditions of supervised -- -- unconstitutional. You can could say it exceeds the statute. The statute is very broad about reasonably necessary. Yeah, it's just got a lot of, you know, yada, yada, yada about kinds of stuff. But, when it gets to this kind of stuff, which is just weird stuff like, you know, go to church -- castration seems a little bit outside the statute. One of them said the defendant was getting so many women pregnant out of wedlock -- this is a federal court -- and said, if you're going to get someone pregnant, can you please make it your wife? You know, you just can't do that. Come on, that's silly. Counsel, how much of this -- It's just -- you just can't do that. And that's unauthorized by the supervised release statute. And then anything beyond that? I just want to have a defined list if we're going to do this. So what cabins it is the first part. You can't just say, well, I have -- you know, I don't want to talk to my probation officer every day because that violates my free speech. You're not even going to get past the first gate, I mean, and you're going to run the risk of getting sanctions. So all that kind of garbage is out. Ms. Blatt -- And then you -- if I could finish. Yeah. Please. Sorry. On your -- in your beginning, you said clear legal error. And now that seems to open up -- because everyone thinks their legal error is clear, open up a wider box. And I just want to make sure -- So, no, because you can say, like, mandamus, clear and indisputable, clearly established, plain error, the error has to be obvious, clear. And that's what the courts below say. You can even say it louder. I mean, you -- you get -- you get to say what you want. Well, some courts say that and some courts don't. There's -- that's why we're here. There's a split. Some -- I will be honest, some are really broad and just say any illegal sentence. And guess what, there's no flood, there's no appeals. There's 30 years of this. The first -- I'm not disputing you. Okay. Okay. I'm sorry. These are not hostile questions. (Laughter.) So -- okay. The thing is I -- I trust the system on the three systemic reasons -- Yeah. -- because there's an appeal waiver. Yeah. And the court of appeals don't want to see these, and lawyers, you know, are very careful in bringing them. On terms of clear error, I do think it's like the second prong of Olano. It's just plain error. It's easy. It's applied every day in forfeiture. No one has a problem misunderstanding that. Are you essentially endorsing the Fourth Circuit's test, which is a fundamental constitutional or statutory right that was firmly established at the time of sentencing? Is that what you're saying to Justice Kavanaugh? I like that. I mean, yeah, that sounds good. I hadn't heard that one, but, yeah, I just think in terms of Justice -- Fourth Circuit's -- that's the Fourth Circuit's standard. I'm just trying to get Justice Alito's vote, and what I'm trying to say -- (Laughter.) -- to Justice Alito is -- I care about the rest of you too, but -- Thank you very much. (Laughter.) It's very -- very few advocates have that -- I'll just stop then. (Laughter.) -- goal. Ms. Blatt -- Sorry. -- I'm -- I'm trying to figure out how we articulate this, okay? You've come in with a simple proposition that ordinary contract principles, defenses should generally apply. There might be some -- The same standard the government has. The same standard the government has. And that's not just frustration of purpose because frustration of purpose means both a procedural and substantive component. And you may not have a procedural component in this kind of waiver. But I think the other defense are policy, public policy, it's against public policy. That's the rationale for statutory maximums, which is Congress has said you should only receive a sentence of X amount, okay? That's what you get. Yeah. And there's separation of powers issues. Yeah. Exactly. Unconscionability. I think it depends on your comfort level with those two words. All right. But I think -- A lot of people freak out at that word. I don't because -- I know, but I don't either. Okay. And the implied duty of good faith, that has to do with a judge doing what he's supposed to do, and that subsumes unconscionability -- that subsumes -- Yes, and -- -- clear error. Yes, and -- It subsumes constitutional error. And is a heavy thumb on the -- the implied -- parties' expectation that the contract would be enforced. So what I think what the government -- the scare tactics, they sound really broad. They're not because, if you just read one Delaware case, it'll tell you the implied covenant of good faith has to mean -- All right. Let me -- let me just stop you on all of this discussion. Okay. Arizona, Minnesota, California, and Texas, all of their high courts say that they -- a prospective waiver of a not-yet-imposed sentence is not enforceable, all right, when the defendant does not know what errors, if any, that there could be because they're not giving up a right -- A -- a known -- -- a known right. You haven't argued that. It may be too much water under the bridge, but there is a strong argument, by the way, and it -- and it goes back to something that Justice -- that Justice Gorsuch was referring to -- on the sentencing guidelines. The reports when the guidelines came out said we're permitting appeal waivers because appellate review of sentences is essential to ensure that the guidelines are -- are applied properly and to provide case law development -- development of the reasons for sentencing outside the guidelines. Yeah. Guideline errors are just going to be out. And they've been here for -- I know. But -- but don't give up so easily, okay?
